Dādū
------------------------------------------
The political and social turmoil in medieval India was also responsible—though in a strange and inscrutable way—to throw up many a great saint who tried by their lives and teachings, to show that the true spirit of religion lies in inner mystical experience and not in dry rituals or meaningless formalities.
Dādū (A.
-1603) was one of the brighter स्तर्स् of this period and the most famous of the followers of कबीर्’s (A.

-1518) ideals. Born in Ahmedabad (in Gujarat) he seems to have spent most of his time in Rajasthan. He passed away in the village Narāṇā (or नारायण) of Rajasthan, where his followers—known as ‘Dādūpanthis’—have their chief centre even now.
He established the ‘Brahma or Parabrahma सम्प्रदाय’ with a view to uniting all the divergent faiths in one bond of love and friendship.
He did not believe in the authority of the scriptures but in the value of realisation. He laid great stress on the cultivation of virtues like humility, compassion, fearlessness, forgiveness and firmness in one’s path.
He was a householder and believed that the natural life of the householder was best suited for spiritual realisation.
His children too (two sons and two daughters) were persons of high spiritual calibre.
At his request, his disciples made (in A.

) a collection of the devotional writings of all the different sects. This anthology, containing the sayings of many Muslim saints also, helped the spiritual aspirants of all types in their journey towards perfection.
See also KABĪR.
